cras.name: Panama City CRA
cras.overview: The Panama City Community Redevelopment Agency was created in 1983. The City Commission sits as its board, and it currently runs four tax-increment districts: Downtown (1984), St. Andrews (1989, expanded 2025), Downtown North/Glenwood (1993, expanded several times) and Millville (2004). City and Bay County tax increment provided about $1.6M a year in the early 2010s, roughly $1.3M in FY2021 after Hurricane Michael, and about $3.0-3.6M by FY2024-25. The money pays for 50/50 business and residential improvement grants, park and waterfront projects (Millville Waterfront Park, the Bayview Boardwalk, McKenzie Park), streetscape and beautification work, community policing, maintenance MOUs, a 2024 TIF rebate incentive program for private developers, and the 2025 Glenwood Town Center land deal. All districts are scheduled to sunset in 2044.

cras.name: Lynn Haven CRA
cras.overview: The City Commission created the Lynn Haven Community Redevelopment Agency by Resolution 2004-05-351 on May 25, 2004, after a 2003 feasibility study, and the Commission sits as its board. It is a single district of about 695 acres covering the historic 1911-plat core around Ohio and Florida Avenues, with 2003 as the base year. Its work has been modest in scale: storefront, residential infill and paint incentives, park and stormwater work, and from about 2022 onward mostly sidewalk construction, all paid for with city and Bay County tax increment that grew from about $300K a year (FY2017) to about $1.04M (FY2025). The CRA reports no debt. In December 2025 and January 2026 the Commission extended the redevelopment plan and the agency, which had been set to sunset around 2033, to November 30, 2043.

cras.name: Panama City Beach CRA
cras.overview: The Panama City Beach City Council created its Community Redevelopment Agency on November 30, 2000. It then created the Front Beach Road CRA by resolution on June 21, 2001 and adopted the redevelopment plan in August 2001. The plan calls for rebuilding about 19.8 miles of road in phased 'segments': widening, medians, sidewalks, trolley lanes, stormwater work, lighting and undergrounded utilities along Front Beach Road, South Thomas Drive, South Arnold Road (SR 79) and connector roads. Bay County tax increment paid for it, growing from about $0.9M in FY2003 to about $21-22M a year by FY2024-25. The program was also backed by Series 2006 ($54.8M), Series 2015 refunding ($42.9M) and Series 2020 ($35.1M) revenue bonds, and the FY2024-25 budget books interest on Series 2024 bonds. A separate 93-acre Pier Park CRA passes its tax increment, and most of its business-tax receipts, to the Pier Park Community Development District under a 2001 agreement with The St. Joe Company. The Front Beach Road plan was extended from 2031 to 2049 in 2019, which led to years of dispute with Bay County over cost. That ended in a 2024 agreement capping annual CRA revenue at $30M.

cras.name: Callaway CRA
cras.overview: The Callaway Community Redevelopment Agency is a dependent district and blended component unit of the City of Callaway, with the City Commission serving as its board. It was created by City Ordinance 829 (audits give May 8, 2007) and adopted its redevelopment plan by Resolution 07-13 in 2007. The district covers roughly 1,400 acres in the commercial core along Tyndall Parkway (US-98) and Highway 22. Tax increment was small until about FY2021, then rose quickly to more than $1.1 million in FY2025, while spending lagged far behind budget. Fund balance therefore grew to about $2.25 million by the end of FY2025.

cras.name: Springfield CRA
cras.overview: The Springfield Community Redevelopment Agency was created by Resolution/Ordinance 07-05 on March 30, 2007. It is a component unit of the City of Springfield, and the City Commission sits as its board. The base taxable value was about $67.6 million; by February 2025 the area was valued at about $118.4 million. For several years the CRA collected TIF but spent nothing, and auditors found the City had not transferred its own share of the increment for FY2022-2024. Recent budgets put the built-up reserves toward park and sidewalk projects (Springfield Gardens Walking Park, Nature Park, Buddy McLemore Park, Carrie Bell Shaw Park, and 2nd/3rd Street sidewalks).

cras.name: Parker CRA
cras.overview: The Community Redevelopment Agency of the City of Parker was established May 25, 2004, by City Council Resolution 2004-05-350. It is a dependent district governed by the City Council. For most of its history it had no positive tax increment: it received $0 TIF in FY2023 and ran a tiny budget for audit costs. Increment collection finally began in FY2024 ($247,539) and grew in FY2025 ($393,198), with spending so far limited to reimbursing the City.

controversies.text: Michael Johnson, the city's former community development director, was charged in 2021 with embezzling from the Friends of After School Assistance Program. In March 2023 he pleaded no contest to grand theft, money laundering and 19 counts of official misconduct and was sentenced to 8 years. The CRA's FY2022 audit says a former key employee was convicted of misappropriating $83,390 from the Downtown North CRA, and it restated the prior year's financial statements for fraud-related disallowed costs.

Warren Averett's forensic audit (reported June 2023) concluded Johnson acted alone. It found roughly $89,000 taken from the CRA and about $1 million from Friends of ASAP, and found that CRA money was used to renovate four of his personal rental properties, which the city seized to sell.

Audited statements for several years show internal inconsistencies. The tax increment figure in Note 1 does not match the revenue statements in FY2021-FY2024, and FY2023 expenditures exceeded appropriations by $935,842.

The 447 Harrison Ave breezeway was acquired through a land swap with investor George Kingston's company and renovated with CRA funds. Its plans changed several times, budgets ranged from $81,000 to $700,000 across documents, and in 2025 officials considered selling it to a developer.

During the 2025 St. Andrews expansion, some residents questioned whether inclusion in the CRA would benefit their properties. Bay County approved the expansion only after negotiating to keep 26% of the increment from the new area.

The CRA discontinued its business grant programs in September 2023 and later reopened them only for hardship cases. The board approved a multi-year, $4.5M in-house road repair plan on a 3-2 vote, with Josh Street and Robbie Hughes dissenting.

On Nov 20, 2019, federal prosecutors (N.D. Fla.) indicted former City Manager Michael White, Community Services/Leisure Services Director David Horton, Erosion Control Specialists (ECS) owner David 'Mickey' White, ECS employee Shannon Rodriguez and Greenleaf Lawn Care owner Joshua Anderson. The charges alleged about $5 million in fraudulent Hurricane Michael cleanup invoices to the City of Lynn Haven. These were city hurricane-recovery and FEMA-related funds, not CRA tax increment. All five pleaded guilty; Horton was the last, on July 14, 2020. In 2023 Michael White and David White each received 42 months in prison, Horton and Joshua Anderson 9 months of home confinement plus probation, and Rodriguez probation.

On Aug 18, 2020, a federal grand jury indicted Mayor Margo Anderson and City Attorney Adam Albritton on 64 counts, including fraud tied to ECS cleanup and trash-pickup billing. The alleged amounts included more than $48,000 of work at Anderson-linked homes and about $1.8M billed for trash pickup. Albritton pleaded guilty to wire fraud and honest-services wire fraud in September 2021 and in early 2024 was sentenced to probation and about $31,000 in restitution. Anderson pleaded guilty in February 2023 to one count of lying to the FBI and was sentenced on June 5, 2023 to one month in prison plus probation. None of the charges, as reported, involved CRA funds.

A March 2021 superseding indictment charged developer James Finch (Phoenix Construction) and former Commissioner Antonius Barnes. It concerned the 17th Street ditch stormwater project, reported as a 2015 contract of about $3.72M later financed by a 30-year city promissory note to Finch exceeding $5M in principal, and a 2017 half-cent infrastructure surtax design/build contract under which Phoenix was paid $5.6M. It also covered debris disposal and a proposed post-storm municipal building rebuild. These were city surtax, note-financed and hurricane-related projects; no source found ties them to the CRA trust fund. Barnes pleaded guilty to an unrelated bank-loan fraud count and in June 2023 was sentenced to 45 days in prison. Finch's first trial ended in a hung jury, and he was acquitted on Oct 26, 2023.

Reporting on the case said ECS took part in a sham bid for work at Sheffield Park, the downtown park that the CRA had budgeted to improve ($380,000 for Phase II courtyard and stage in FY2018). No source found says CRA dollars paid ECS. Separately, residents questioned more than $330,000 paid to ECS for post-storm cleanup at James E. Rogers Park, which lies outside the CRA. That money was storm-recovery spending, not CRA money.

On Dec 9, 2025 the City Commission voted unanimously to extend the CRA redevelopment plan (Resolution 2025-12-496), and on Jan 13, 2026 it extended the agency to Nov 30, 2043 (Resolution 2026-01-504). Critics argued the CRA had outlived its purpose and its projects were moving slowly. Supporters pointed to the business incentives and to the roughly $668,000 in county tax increment the city would lose in FY2026 without the CRA.

In September 2019 the City Council voted 3-2 to extend the Front Beach Road CRA plan from 2031 to 2049. Bay County had asked for a delay to negotiate first. News coverage projected about $800M in county-funded payments through 2049 if trends held, and a county commissioner warned the county might have to raise millage. Two council members opposed the extension.

In March 2020 the city and county approved an interlocal agreement (Res. 20-85). The CRA would rebate 20% of county tax increment above $15M a year, and new post-2020 borrowing counted toward fixed obligations only up to $80M. The agreement noted that the county's projected contribution, over $700M, far exceeded original estimates.

In 2023 Bay County raised its millage for the first time in about a decade. Some commissioners blamed the beach CRA, and the county said CRAs could absorb up to 20% of its tax revenue. The PCB mayor accused the commission of spreading misinformation. One commissioner said the county had paid $172M through 2023 and estimated about $586M in savings if projects finished 11 years early. Another commissioner called for ending the CRA.

In 2024 the city and county agreed to cap annual CRA revenue at $30M through 2049. Reports estimated the cap would save the county about $2.7B over 25 years, with the cap expected to bind around 2028-2029.
The city used eminent domain repeatedly for Segment 3, 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3 right-of-way. Examples include 17138/17140 Front Beach Rd and the 16726 FBR leasehold, after voluntary purchase talks failed.

Businesses complained about long construction disruptions on Segment 2 (2016-2019) and Segment 3 (2021-2026). Segment 3 ran about 375 days late because of utility conflicts and a storm-drain redesign. One restaurant owner described parking problems and a lawsuit with the city, and said several businesses closed during construction.

The Segment 3 construction contract was awarded to GAC Contractors in 2021 and assigned to CWR Contracting (C.W. Roberts) in April 2022, shortly after work began. Project cost grew from an FY2019 estimate of $24.3M (including land) to roughly $31-32.5M.

In FY2015 the city rejected all Segment 2 bids because the low bid far exceeded the budget, and re-bid the project in 2016. In 2021 the Powell Adams Road Segment II bids also came in over the CRA budget.

Year after year, CRA spending ran far below budget. FY2025 capital outlay was about $316K against a $3.14M budget, so the restricted fund balance built up to about $2.25M. Audits blamed delayed property rehab and spillway projects and business grants with no applicants.

The FY2024 audit reported a material weakness: the City had not calculated or transferred its required share of the tax increment to the CRA for FY2022-2024, an estimated $291,027. The auditor attributed this to a lack of understanding of the requirement.

The FY2025 audit repeated the finding on late City transfers, estimating the cumulative underfunding at $526,519. A catch-up transfer was made in September 2025. The audit also found the CRA had not sent its budgets to Bay County within the 10 days required by s.163.387(6), F.S.
The 2024 annual report said none of the redevelopment plan's goals had yet been met and no projects had been completed. Reserves were only being built up at that point.
The FY2024 audit found the City of Parker had not transferred its required TIF contribution to the CRA for FY2024, an estimated shortfall of $78,568 (finding 2024-001).

gaps.text: No district-level TIF or budget figures were found for FY1984-FY2009, FY2012-FY2013 or FY2019-FY2020 (the FY2019 and FY2020 audits on flauditor.gov were unreadable or failed to load). Older annual reports and audits likely sit in the panamacity.gov Document Center or Archive Center, or can be had by records request.

Grant recipient names are mostly missing before FY2024. Annual reports give aggregate 50/50 grant totals. Grant agreements and check registers would require a public records request to the CRA (cras@panamacity.gov).
Price and seller for the April 2017 purchase of 37 lots and 35 homes on 6.5 acres in Downtown North. Check Bay County property appraiser and clerk deed records.

The CRA's share of the roughly $7M Harrison Ave streetscape (2021-2025). Public sources cite a $5.7M state agreement and $5.6M CDBG-DR Project HEART but no CRA amount. Check CRA board agendas for 2021-2025.
Final terms and sale price of the 2025 Sankofa Group Glenwood Town Center agreement (the proposal offered $667,099.62). The development agreement is in the July 2025 CRA agenda packet.

Contract values for consultants (GAI Consultants plan update, AECOM marina master plan, Retail Strategies actuals) and for construction contractors (Mainline Construction, CBC Construction, VBA/Florida Architects).

Downtown Marina/Bay County Marina and St. Andrews Marina rebuilds appear to be funded mainly by the city, FEMA and grants. No CRA payment amounts were found. The 2026 St. Andrews Marina cost-plus contract amount was not reported.

Hurricane Michael recovery: CDBG-DR Hometown Revitalization facade grants ($20.1M across CRA corridors) are city/state funds, not CRA TIF, so they are excluded from payments. CRA-specific post-storm spending in FY2019-2020 is undocumented online.

No Glenwood, Bayou George/Lake Caroline or Cove/East CRA districts exist as separate districts. Glenwood is part of Downtown North. The Cove area got a $12.949M city contract, but no CRA district covers it.

No vendor-level CRA check register was found. Annual reports give program totals with unnamed payees. A public-records request for Fund 701 (dept 559) disbursements from the city Finance Dept would supply payees.
FY2005-FY2016 budgets, tax increment and expenditures were not found online. Older city budgets and audits (Carr, Riggs & Ingram) would have them, as would the city clerk's CRA minutes.

The FY2017/18 and FY2022/23 CRA annual reports and the FY2022-23 and FY2024-25 standalone CRA budgets are listed on the city CRA page but could not be retrieved. FY2023 figures here come from the Auditor General filing and the city midyear budget.

The FY2025-26 approved CRA budget is a poor-quality scan. Line items such as the Illinois and Minnesota sidewalks, the Porter Park kayak launch, Memorial Park, Griffin playground and the storefront allocation were not legible, so the FY2026 tax increment figure is left blank.
Actual spending on the Sharon Sheffield Park Phase II courtyard and stage, which was budgeted at $380,000 in FY2018, was not confirmed.
Addresses of storefront grant and residential incentive recipients were not disclosed. Only 520 Ohio Ave (a hardware store, FY2017) was identified.
Whether the $50,300 for Roberts Hall and McMullin Library in FY2020 was entirely CRA money is unclear.
The CRA share of the $623,137.69 Tennessee Ave sidewalk contract, which is FDOT LAP funded, is not stated.

The original 2004 Community Redevelopment Plan (PDF on the city site) and the 2025 plan amendment were not reviewed in detail. They would contain the base-year value, finding of necessity and project lists.
No evidence was found of CRA bonds or debt. Auditor General filings for FY2021-FY2025 state no legal indebtedness.

Several topics turned up nothing tying them to the Lynn Haven CRA: a marina or bayfront/Bayview Ave project, a 'Mosaic' or Main Street program, a CRA-funded city hall or civic center, and CRA property purchases. The 17th Street ditch, the sports complex and the city hall rebuild were city, surtax or hurricane-recovery projects.

Annual adopted CRA budget totals for FY2003-FY2016, FY2019-FY2021 and FY2026 were not found. They likely sit in budget resolutions (e.g., Res. 19-137, 22-211, 23-217) and city budget books on pcbfl.gov.

Actual revenues and expenditures are known only for some years: FY2020 revenue $13,085,513; FY2021 revenue $14,592,537 and expenditures $16,634,476; FY2022 $15,303,477 and $15,242,194; FY2023 $20,608,513 and $20,383,756; FY2024 $31,156,153 and $22,111,115; FY2025 $26,522,556 and $17,543,945. Full statements are in the city ACFRs and the Exhibit A financial statements, which did not extract.

The original Segment 3 construction contract amount (Res. 21-127, March 25, 2021) and the amounts of CWR Change Orders 1-6 were not found. The resolution PDFs on the city site are image scans with no text. The city's Segment 3 page gives only a low bid of about $28M.
The contractor and contract details for the South Thomas Dr / FBR Segment 1 construction (2009-2011) and the Richard Jackson Blvd contract (c. 2009) were not found.
Corradino Group, DRMP and PBS&J program-management fees are missing, along with Keystone, Morgenstern Phifer Messina, Rogers Valuation and Diskin contract amounts. They are in agenda backup packets.

Individual right-of-way purchase prices and condemnation awards are missing, apart from the $22,239.36 Palmetto and $31,882.50 PCBH settlements (e.g., Res. 22-200, 23-203 final payments for Segment 4.1, and the 4.2 and 4.3 parcels). They would be in resolutions and Bay County circuit court eminent-domain case files.

Official statements and annual disclosures for the Series 2006, 2015 and 2020 bonds, and whether the Series 2024 bonds were issued (FY2024-25 budgets book 2024-bond interest), were not checked on EMMA (emma.msrb.org). Underwriters and interest rates are therefore unknown.
The construction award for Segments 4.1-4.3 is still pending. Design-build proposals for Segment 4.1 were due Oct 22, 2026, so no contractor or amount is available yet.
Total Bay County rebates paid under the 2020 interlocal agreement, and the text of the 2024 $30M cap agreement, were not found. Bay County BOCC minutes would have them.

No CRA spending was found for City Pier/Aaron Bessant Park, beach access parks or trolley operations. Those appear to be city or other funds. In 2011 the CRA sought $9M in NRDA funds for a Long Beach Access Park; whether it was funded is unknown.
Pier Park CDD bond amounts and debt schedules were not found. Pier Park CDD audits filed with the Florida Auditor General would have them.

Callaway's CRA annual reports (for example the 2023 annual report), CRA agendas and minutes, and budget resolutions (CRA Res 2021-01) are on cityofcallaway.com, but that site couldn't be read by our tools. These would name vendors and projects.
No vendor-level payments were found. Check the CRA board agenda packets in the city AgendaCenter.

No CRA audit for FY2020 or earlier could be found on the Auditor General's site. Pre-2021 tax increment history (2007-2020) is unknown apart from FY2021's $54,221, taken from the FY2022 audit comparison.
The 2007 Redevelopment Plan PDF on the city site returned an error, so planned project costs and the sunset date were not captured.

The Tyndall Parkway median beautification (2019-2020, $500K, Lawnscapes Inc.) and the Cherry Street rehab ($5M) were reported as state/FDOT funded with no CRA funding mentioned, so they are excluded. Confirm whether any CRA money went in.
There is no confirmed CRA tie to the Callaway Arts & Conference Center.
Adopted CRA budget totals for FY2024-FY2027 were not found.

Several Springfield PDFs are scans with no text: the FY24-25 budget, Res 2025-02 and Res 2025-03, and the minutes for Nov 2024, May 2025 and Sept 2025. Their line items and vendor awards have not been transcribed yet.
The audit for FY2023 and earlier and TIF history for 2007-2022 were not found. Check the Florida Auditor General special district e-file or City of Springfield ACFRs.
No vendor or contractor names were found for the park and sidewalk projects. The amounts listed are budget appropriations, not paid invoices.
No CRA spending on the Transmitter Rd or 15th St corridor was documented.
Exact park coordinates (Nature Park, Carrie Bell Shaw Park, Buddy McLemore Park) are not geocoded.
TIF and budget history for 2004-2022 was not found. The CRA reportedly had no positive increment for years. Check older Auditor General filings and City of Parker ACFRs.

Parker CRA budget documents for FY2025-FY2027 and any annual reports were not found online (cityofparker.com wp-content uploads may hold them). The FY2025 budget had $286,253 for economic environment, none of it spent.
The redevelopment plan text and any Hwy 98 corridor project list were not found.
The FY2023 Parker CRA audit URL returned an error.
